messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Vinh Tran

Vinh Tran was fifty-eight when the accident happened at the Grandview Hotel, where he had worked his way up from bellhop to general manager over thirty-two years. On a Tuesday morning in March, a contractor's crew had been treating the basement for mold remediation. Vinh had not been notified of the specific chemicals being used—a mixture of industrial-grade fungicide and a solvent that, when combined with residual moisture in the ventilation system, created a toxic vapor. He descended to check on a water leak near the boiler room around 9 a.m., before the extraction fans were properly running. Within minutes, his throat constricted. His eyes burned as if someone had poured acid into them. He could taste it—a sharp, metallic, acrid taste that coated his tongue and throat—and he could not spit it out fast enough. His vision blurred. His heart raced. He stumbled back up the stairs, gasping, convinced he was suffocating, that his lungs were being chemically eaten from the inside. The paramedics arrived within twelve minutes. He spent four days in the hospital. Physically, the doctors said, he would recover fully. The exposure had been acute but not lethal. He was discharged with instructions to rest and follow up with occupational health.

Two years later, Vinh had not recovered in the way the doctors had promised. What had begun as hypervigilance in the weeks after the exposure had calcified into a rigid system of monitoring and avoidance that now governed nearly every hour of his day. He had come to believe that his body could not be trusted—that it had betrayed him once and could do so again without warning. This conviction that his own physiology was unreliable fed directly into an exhausting regimen of surveillance: he checked his skin obsessively for rashes or discoloration, pressed his fingers against his lymph nodes, monitored his breathing for any irregularity. He kept a symptom diary. He took his temperature multiple times daily. He had purchased an air quality monitor for his home and another for his office at the hotel, checking the readings compulsively throughout the day. He was certain that something else was wrong with him—something the initial medical tests had missed—and this certainty that he was helpless to prevent another catastrophe drove him to scan his environment constantly, to position himself near exits, to notice every smell, every unusual sound in the ventilation system. At the hotel, where he had once moved through the corridors with ease and authority, he now felt like an intruder in a place that had become fundamentally unsafe. He no longer belonged in the spaces he had helped build.

The intrusive memories had worsened over the past six months. Without warning—while he was reviewing staff schedules, while he was eating dinner with his partner Maria, while he was trying to sleep—the memory would force itself into his mind with the vividness of something happening in real time. He would taste that chemical taste again, acrid and suffocating, coating his tongue. His body would respond as if he were back in that basement, his heart accelerating, his muscles tensing, his breath becoming shallow. The memory felt like a reliving, not a recollection. When these episodes occurred, his threat detection system would spike; his body, already held in constant tension, would tighten further, and he would scan his surroundings urgently for the source of danger, even though the rational part of him knew the threat was in the past. The vividness of the taste, the involuntary way the memory returned, the sensation of reliving the event—all of this reinforced his conviction that his body was unreliable, that something was fundamentally wrong with him that he could not control or prevent.

This belief in his own helplessness and bodily untrustworthiness had become the engine driving his maladaptive strategies. Because he could not trust his body, he monitored it constantly. Because he felt he could not stop bad things from happening, he scanned his environment obsessively and avoided any reminder of the event—he had not returned to the basement of the hotel in two years, had instructed staff never to mention the incident, and had begun avoiding certain areas of the hotel where the smell of cleaning chemicals triggered panic. His constant vigilance and body-checking, in turn, kept him hyperalert. Every delay—a late delivery, a slow response from maintenance—triggered the thought that something bad was happening, that disaster was unfolding. His body remained in a state of readiness that never resolved. The false alarms were frequent: a faint smell would send him into a panic, convinced he was being exposed again; a momentary chest tightness would convince him that his lungs were failing. And each time his threat system fired without real danger materializing, the memory would intrude—the taste would return, the sensation of reliving the event would wash over him—which would then deepen his conviction that he could not trust his own perceptions, that his body was a liability, that he was helpless. The cycle had become self-perpetuating.

Maria had noticed the changes. He had become withdrawn, checking his phone constantly for health articles, retreating to their bedroom when guests visited. He had lost weight. His hands trembled slightly when he held a glass. At the hotel, his assistant manager had begun handling more of his duties; Vinh found himself unable to concentrate, unable to trust that the building was safe, unable to move through the public spaces without feeling surveilled by his own body. He had taken two extended leaves of absence in the past year. What frightened him most was that the vigilance was not protecting him—it was only exhausting him, only deepening his certainty that he was trapped in a body that could turn on him at any moment, in a world where danger could arrive without warning and where he was powerless to stop it. It was Maria who finally insisted he seek help, who said that she could not watch him disappear any longer. That was what had brought Vinh to the psychologist's office: the recognition that the strategies he had built to survive the exposure were now the very things that were destroying his life.
